items.title: 21.1.2 Defence Provided by Digestive and Respiratory Tracts

source_refs.note: Topic 21.1.2 (PDF 171-172); Figure 21.3 is replaced by the original diagram.

blocks.text: Food carries many bacteria. Most are killed by saliva in the mouth, which also contains lysozyme, and by the strong acid in the stomach and the protein-digesting enzymes of the intestine.

The air we breathe also carries many microbes. Ciliated epithelial cells in the nasal cavity trap many bacteria before they enter the airway. The cells lining the smaller bronchi and bronchioles secrete sticky mucus that traps microbes before they reach the warm, moist lungs, and cilia on these cells keep sweeping the mucus upward, where it can be swallowed.

blocks.alt: A strip of tracheal epithelium: columnar cells with mucous cells among them, cilia on their free surface, and a mucous layer over the cilia with trapped microbes in it. An upward arrow shows the movement of mucus. A small inset shows the head, trachea and lungs, with a box on the trachea.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.3: Epithelium of trachea, with trapped microbes (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.3).
